title: Minimal evidence exchange playbook for customer VPC onboarding
content:
Purpose
This is a working PRD draft for a lightweight, bandwidth-aware audit and approval exchange between Redwood and customer-managed VPCs during onboarding and subsequent network changes. The goal is to define a minimal set of artifacts, an approval handshake, and runtime sampling rules that keep regulatory and forensic requirements satisfied while minimizing on-prem bandwidth and customer privacy exposure.

Problem statement
- Large forensic bundles and full syslog exports create operational friction for customers with low-bandwidth or metered links (edge sites, offshore datacenters).
- Our existing proposals assume always-on telemetry exports; customers ask for smaller, deterministic packages during handoff and change events.
- Security/compliance teams want tamper-evident receipts tied to approval decisions but do not want full packet-level logs leaving their VPC.

High-level proposal
We will introduce a Minimal Evidence Exchange (MEE) pattern composed of:
1) Compact audit slices: small, compressed, signed JSON-LD style bundles that summarize a change event or a handoff snapshot. Each slice contains an index (operation id, timestamp, change hash), metadata (actor, owner contact, change scope labels), and a tiny, privacy-safe digest of what changed (e.g., ACL delta fingerprints, route table identifiers, security-group rule hashes).
2) Micro-approval tokens: short-lived, cryptographically-signed tokens representing an approval decision (canary vs full) with a TTL and a link to the relevant compact slice. Tokens are exchangeable between customer operator consoles and Redwood for rollback triggers and SLA enforcement.
3) Bandwidth-aware delivery modes: immediate push for large-capacity customers, store-and-forward for constrained links (batching multiple slices in a single compact bundle on a cadence), and on-demand pull for forensic investigations.
4) Sparse sampling policy and deterministic retention: to reduce noise, we adopt configurable sampling rates for non-critical events and guarantee retention windows for slices used in SA/contractual investigations.

User journeys (skeletal)
A. Initial onboarding handshake (operator-driven)
- Customer operator requests a Redwood private deployment onboarding.
- Temporary operator attestation requested: customer generates an initial Compact Snapshot slice describing current network boundary (list of external CIDRs, NAT gateways, edge appliances identified by nonce). Slice is signed by customer key and uploaded to Redwood's onboarding endpoint.
- Redwood validates slice, issues a micro-approval token (initial-ack) with TTL 48h. Token indicates agreed SLO for evidence exchange and a preferred delivery mode (push/pull).
- Customer accepts token; onboarding moves to network tests. Token recorded in immutable approval ledger.

B. Routine change with low bandwidth link
- Operator submits a change via their console; the console emits a Change Delta slice (compact) and signs it locally.
- If link constrained, console queues slice and attaches a local sequence number; slices are batched hourly into a single bundle with a manifest. Each bundle retains individual slice signatures and a bundle-level signature.
- Redwood verifies signatures on receipt (or when pulled). If change exceeds risk threshold per policy, Redwood returns a micro-approval token requiring operator confirmation before rollout.

C. Emergency rollback
- Detection (on either side) triggers an emergency flow that can consume the micro-approval token and the relevant slice(s). The token acts as an allowlist for rollback actions; bundle proves the pre-change state.

Design details and constraints
- Slice size target: <= 8 KB per change slice for typical ACL/route deltas. Bundle target: <= 256 KB when batched. These targets are soft; telemetry will measure distribution and we'll iterate.
- Signing: ECDSA-P256 signatures using customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Redwood stores only the public key and verifies signatures; private keys never leave customer control (when using customer KMS).
- Hashing: changes are represented as canonicalized JSON and fingerprinted with SHA-256. We store the hash to enable compact cross-references without storing full payloads.
- Privacy: slices must omit payloads (PII, payload metadata) and only include structural identifiers and hashes. Any raw metadata requiring retention for compliance is negotiated per-customer.
- Transport: HTTPS with mutual TLS or pre-signed upload URLs; store-and-forward mode supports signed bundles dropped into an s3-compatible endpoint with clearly documented retention and access policies.

Approval gate semantics
- Gates are policy-driven and configurable per tenant: low/medium/high risk mappings to required approvals (auto-approve with token, require human approval, require multi-party approval).
- Micro-approval tokens contain: operation_id, risk_level, approver_ids, TTL, applicable_slice_hash, signature. Tokens are single-use for rollback flows but can be renewed for follow-ups.
- Auditability: every token issuance, renewal, revocation, or consumption is written to Redwood's immutable approval ledger with references to slice hashes (not full slices). Ledger entries include a short human-readable summary for faster triage.

APIs and example payloads (sketch)
- POST /v1/onboard/slices  -- upload a signed compact snapshot
  body: signed_slice (base64), metadata: { operator_email, tenant_id, delivery_mode_hint }
- POST /v1/onboard/bundles -- upload a signed bundle (store-and-forward)
  body: { bundle_manifest: [slice_hashes], signatures: [base64], bundle_size_bytes }
- GET /v1/approval/token/{token_id} -- fetch token metadata (status, TTL)
- POST /v1/approval/consume -- consume token for rollback
  body: { token_id, operation_hash, consumer_identity, reason }

(We will produce a proto contract after initial signoff; above are placeholders for the UX and error model.)

Acceptance criteria
- Redwood successfully verifies and stores 95% of slices under 8 KB without requiring rehydration of full logs (measured in onboarding sandbox).
- Micro-approval token lifecycle test passes: issuance, renewal, revocation, consumption flows covered in e2e tests.
- Bandwidth batching reduces bytes transmitted by at least 60% for constrained-customer synthetic trace versus naive full-syslog export.
- UX checklist: operator can view last 10 slices, token status, and request immediate pull in < 3 clicks in the console prototype.

Operational considerations
- Backwards compatibility: existing customers on full-syslog exports can opt into MEE; Redwood must support dual-mode export for 90 days during migration.
- Monitoring: add per-tenant metrics: slice_rate, average_slice_size, bundle_success_rate, token_issue_rate, token_error_rate.
- Alerts: failed signature verifications >1% in 10-minute window triggers a pager to eng-private-deployments.

Security & compliance notes
- Legal review required for jurisdictions that prohibit export of certain flow metadata; MEE will provide an opt-out where only hashes are transmitted and Redwood can run zero-knowledge verification protocols with customer auditors on request.
- Key rotation: support automated rotation of customer public keys with a 7-day overlap window to avoid failed verifications.

Open questions and proposed experiments
- What is the right default sampling policy for low-risk infra events? (proposal: 1 in 10, sample jittered by tenant)
- Can we prototype a zero-knowledge proof that asserts that an ACL delta doesn't expose blocked CIDRs without sending CIDR lists? (R&D spike)
- UX: should micro-approval tokens be visible in mobile operator apps? Quick test: push prototype to 3 customers with edge sites.

Next steps (immediate)
- Product: align with legal on export opt-outs and retention windows (owner: Mariana).
- Eng infra: prototype compact slice canonicalizer and signer library (owner: Tomás).
- Eng security: design token signing and approval ledger schema (owner: Evan).
- Solutions: identify 2 pilot customers for constrained-link trials (owner: Ritika).

Notes to reviewers
This is a draft focused on pragmatic, smallest-possible artifacts and flows for regulated customers with constrained connectivity. Feedback requested on:
- slice size targets and bundle cadence
- approval token semantics and single-use policy
- compatibility with existing customer-managed KMS setups

Revision history
- 2024-11-18 initial draft
- 2024-12-03 added API sketches and acceptance criteria
